Uniform Title: Sambandhasiddhi Secondary Title: Siddhitrayī Author: Utpaladeva

Description: An e-text transcribed from volume 34 of the Kashmir Series of Texts and Studies, wherein it is bound together with other works of Utpaladeva: the *Ājaḍapramātṛsiddhi*, the *Īśvarasiddhi*, and the *Īśvarapratyabhijñākārikāvṛtti*. The *Sambandhasiddhi*, *Ājaḍapramātṛsiddhi*, and *Īśvarasiddhi* are collectively known as the *Siddhitrayī*.

Notes: This electronic text was transcribed by the staff of Muktabodha under the supervision of Mark S.G. Dyczkowski. Revision 0: November 28, 2005. Publisher: Research Department, Jammu and Kashmir State. Year of publication: 1921.
Place of publication: Srinagar;
Country of publication: India.
Now.
The *Saṃbandhasiddhi*,
composed by the venerable teacher Utpaladeva,
which establishes all objects through the relationship consisting of both difference and non-difference.
We praise that Śiva, whose worldly course is performed according to his own will. || 1 ||

Victorious is the one Supreme Lord, the Light who is the soul of the universe, even though he manifests a body composed of the relationship between the various states of being and their distinctions. (2)

Here, the relation between entities is being investigated. First of all, what is the meaning of the word "relation"? Even when one says "conjunction" (*saṃsarga*), "contact" (*saṃparka*), "adhesion" (*saṃśleṣa*), or "relation" (*saṃbandha*), the meaning of "relation" is not clearly elucidated. What [is it]?
Is continuity (nairantarya) conjunction (saṃśleṣa), or is it something else? If it were continuity, then it would not exist between a father and son standing at a distance;
yet it would exist even between two iron rods placed close together, and even between all-pervading substances (vibhudravya). Now, suppose it resides in both [the things conjoined].

A category (*padārtha*) is a certain relation. If, in that case as well, being a relation consists solely in residing in two things (*dviṣṭhatā*), then that [status of being a relation] would also apply to duality (*dvitva*), separateness (*dvipṛthaktva*), and so forth. But this is not the intended meaning.

The word "relation" (saṃbandha) arises not by conforming to the meanings of its constituent parts—though some manuscripts read *etad uttiṣṭhati*—but rather, like the word *tailapāyikā*, solely through convention (*saṃketa*). Furthermore, the meaning of the word "relation" itself is not even "dual-residence" (*dviṣṭhatā*). Rather...

That [relation], being distinct from the two [relata] alone, exists only when the two are connected; thus it is said to "reside in both" (*dviṣṭha*). In that case, let that relation be clearly stated in its own nature as *saṃśleṣa* (conjunction).

This is the meaning of these and other such synonyms. Furthermore, dependence (*pāratantrya*) and the like are not distinct meanings of "relation" (*saṃbandha*); rather, that meaning would be implied by the very principle of its residing in two things (*dviṣṭhatva*).
Nor is this [dependence] implied by the sense, for the meaning of dependence does not apply to two insentient correlates.

Or, the meaning of "dependence on another" (*pāratantrya*) may be applicable. Even if it is argued that the sprout itself depends upon the seed, or that it is dependent on the seed because its acquisition of self-nature (*ātmalābha*) is contingent upon that [seed], this too is not correct;
for this would be a mere metaphorical expression, as if it were "dependent," whereas in reality, an insentient thing [cannot truly be so].
The primary longing, prayer, or desire itself is indeed a specific kind of expectation (*apekṣā*),

or else it is dependence (*pāratantrya*)— that is, being inclined toward another or the longing for being employed by another; this is logically consistent only as a particular form of volition (*saṃkalpa*) characterized by the cessation of acting according to one's own will.

And for that which has not yet attained its own self, dependence and so forth are spoken of for the sake of attaining that self— [in the Kha manuscript, the reading is "attainment of the object"]— but at that time, because it does not yet exist as a dual entity, the occurrence of a relationship for the sake of connection is not possible.
Therefore, the primary relationship must indeed be stated explicitly.
To this it is replied: "Relationship," "contact," and "conjunction" are synonyms; and that sense of conjunction is said to be the unification of many into one.

But the relation is neither multiplicity alone nor unity alone; rather, this relation depends upon both states. For this very reason, there is no single relation belonging to many. For if the relation were merely multiplicity or merely unity, [it would be untenable].

It might [occur] when many things attain oneness, or even when they do not attain oneness, or it might occur for a single thing alone. However, when the relation of oneness belongs to what is manifold—
In view of both [possibilities], because it depends upon more than one, there is no relation for a single [entity] alone;
and because it depends upon only one, there is no relation for multiple [entities] existing separately. Nor is there a single relation among three or more, for as for the three...

Because they are based on a twofold division governed by distinct differences and are mutually differentiated, and because their existence as related entities depends upon one another; for the unity that one has with a second is not the same as its unity with a third, due to the difference between those two—the second and the third—and because of their mutual dependence. Therefore...

Even for many things numbered in the hundreds and so forth, only a single relationship is proclaimed for each pair; thus, the meaning of the word "relationship" (saṃbandha) as "the one self of two" is established precisely according to its constituent parts. By the prefix *sam-*...

It has indeed been clearly stated that unity consists in the coexistence of many in a single place, preceded by their departure from other locations— whether this coexistence be through a common purpose or a shared objective. The only remaining question is whether such a unity of the many is even possible.
It is considered as follows: therein this relation is perceived in many ways—
as "the son of the father," "the servant of the king," "the branch of the tree," "the dhava and the khadira trees," "the blue lotus," and "Devadatta cooks rice in a pot with firewood."
[It occurs] in such forms as "the absence of a jar," "this is other than that," and so forth;

likewise, even by way of reversal, as in "the father of the son" or "the king of the man. In this regard, is this merely a matter of cognition, or is an object of such a nature actually perceived? Regarding this, if...
"This is merely a matter of conventional cognition; therefore, the true nature of the entity must be stated.
To this, they reply: "An entity such as a jar is complete within its own self-nature and is mutually excluded [from others]; for it is exactly thus."
Conceptual construction (*kalpanā*) is perceived by direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) as manifesting its own nature; thus, that construction is indeed merely imagined.

For they say: "Those entities are themselves unmixed, and conceptual construction joins them together. Likewise, through verbal conceptual construction such as "a blue lotus," there is at most a single identity between the blue and the lotus.
It is cognized,
however, not by that which has as its object the partless particularity of the blue lotus-svalakṣaṇa appearing as a real entity.
By means of the valid cognition of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).
And so they have said:
"Ultimately real objects are conjoined; they do not differ by their own nature."
Form is both one and many; [the notion that it is so] among them is a delusion of the intellect.

And so forth. Furthermore, it is not logical for a unity to coexist with the multiplicity of many things, because they are contradictory by virtue of being of the nature of existence and non-existence. [Nor is it logical] that one arises from multiple material causes, or that many arise from one.

It would arise as entirely unmingled with anything else, terminating solely within itself; just as some maintain the established rule regarding the continuum of consciousness (*vijñānasantati*), for in that case,
[the cognition arises] from the immediately preceding conditions (*samanantarapratyaya*) characterized by the cognitions of sound, touch, and so forth.

Conceptual cognition is based on a single sense-faculty; or else, all five [types of cognition] having sound and so forth as their objects arise from a single immediately preceding condition (*samanantarapratyaya*). Furthermore, that unity and plurality which share a common substratum are sublated by valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), just as the non-existence of an entity would be.

It is solely through this kind of conceptual cognition that objects, although mutually distinct, are presented as having the nature of cause and effect for the sake of accomplishing worldly transactions, even though such a presentation is unreal.

In such cases as "the king and the man" (*rājapuruṣayoḥ*), it is precisely their mutual specific nature and action that are thus defined [in the Kha manuscript, the reading is *nirdiśyate*]; and so too in examples such as "with wood in a pot.
For this very reason, at the very moment of cognition, the relation is accepted just like the universal (*sāmānya*).
And its cognition as being contrary to the actual nature of the object is likewise exclusively an object of error; however, even when sublation occurs,
this [cognition] remains connected with the manifestation of the specific characteristics of the benefactor and the beneficiary.

Just as the delusion of a whole [object] does not cease, like the delusion of a snake, so too this very delusion is designated by the term "conventional" (*saṃvṛti*). To this it is replied: first of all, regarding the cognition [of an object], whether it be of a manifold or a unitary nature—
Indeed, you yourselves have also accepted this for the purpose of expressing a relation, as it has been said:
"Conceptual construction itself joins together those entities which are inherently unmixed."

Thus, its nature as conceptual construction (*kalpanā*) is not a defect. Even the conceptualization "this is a jar," "this is a cloth," and so forth, is indeed conceptual construction. Now, if one argues that here there is also the manifestation of perception (*pratyakṣāvabhāsa*), and since it has the very form of a jar, a cloth, and so on, it is not conceptual construction—here too, [the same applies].

How is it known that even in cases such as "the king's man" (*rājñaḥ puruṣaḥ*) or "rice in the pot" (*sthālyām odanaḥ*), there is no such manifestation as direct perception (*pratyakṣāvabhāsa*)? Furthermore, one must necessarily admit that even here there is a manifestation as direct perception in exactly that way; indeed, you yourselves have already admitted this, since you have stated:
"This error is difficult to dispel even by a subverting cognition (*bādhaka*), because it is closely attached to the appearance of the object's form.

For it is not because of being closely attached to the appearance of the object that it is so, but rather because of the mere existence of a similarity to the appearance of the object; this is the case even in the illusion of silver.

The existence of a similarity with mother-of-pearl is indeed present; for all delusions have similarity as their object (the Kha manuscript reads *sadṛśa* instead of *sādṛśya*), and apart from similarity,
other things are logically connected only by being linked to the appearance of an object.

The very body of the appearance of an object, being of such a nature, is fit to be engaged with by the conceptualizing agent (*vikalpa*) as a conventional user (*vyavahārayitr*) in precisely that form;
otherwise, it would be an appearance of an object rendered into something else entirely.

If [the two terms] are established as resting solely upon their own respective meanings, which do not penetrate into each other's essential nature, then— provided this is the case— this conceptualization of relation would cease, just like the conceptualizations of universals (*sāmānya*) and so forth, and not otherwise. And it is not...

Conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) is distinct from the appearance of the object, because [otherwise] the fault of its being non-conceptual would follow, as stated in the *Īśvarapratyabhijñā*. Likewise, there is such an appearance in cases such as "the king's man."

Thus, a manifestation in the form of the unity of the manifold must be accepted, just like the appearance of a gross object; however, it is only this much that is being investigated— whether or not that [unity] is logically tenable— for in that regard, there is only the ultimate reality whose nature is pure consciousness.

The universal nature of the object: through the power of the creative energy (*māyā-śakti*) of that very pure consciousness (*cinmātra*), by means of the arousal of the non-perception of non-difference,
there arises the mutual differentiation of the universe through its manifold variety consisting of the principles (*tattva*), elements (*bhūta*), worlds (*bhuvana*), and so forth.

This has been explained in detail in the *Īśvarapratyabhijñā*; therefore, it should be examined from that very source and is not set forth here. And when this point is established, the notion of a single, unitary [self] is not tenable.

Since the very cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*) has entered into the meaning of the word "relation," there is no cause for dejection here; rather, this alone is being reflected upon: that because all things are essentially of the nature of a single consciousness, there can be only one relation for the manifold variety of entities—precisely that same relation which exists between a king and his servant.
Regarding the father and son, as well as the pots and so forth, multiplicity is indeed intended. This is stated here as well:

"There may be only one for all. If the relationship were merely oneness itself, then—given that there is multiplicity—the relationship would be oneness through a portion [of that multiplicity]. And therefore:
The relation [of the self] colored by the king’s man is indeed distinct from the relation characterized by the coloring of father and son; for this very reason,
it occurs only in the state of *māyā*, where non-apprehension (*akhyāti*) and difference (*bheda*) predominate.

The existence of the category of relation pertains to the state of being the self of the universe; however, in the state of perfect oneness (*pūrṇaikatā*), there is no further sense of relation whatsoever. Even in that case, occasionally, in the intermediate state (*parāpara-daśā*), because of the requirement for a subordinate aspect, it is used in a figurative sense (*gauṇavṛtti*).

A relation could only exist between two distinct entities that stand in the relationship of benefactor and beneficiary; moreover, such a relation, being of a specific nature, must necessarily be communicated.
If it were not communicated, then those two—the benefactor and the beneficiary—would remain either successive or simultaneous.
Cognition for the purpose of rejection or acquisition would otherwise be impossible;

consequently, worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*) would cease to exist. Furthermore, even between the benefactor and the beneficiary, there is no purpose of benefit that is independent [of consciousness]; this has also been explained in detail in the *Īśvarapratyabhijñā*.
And therefore, it is the very will of the Lord, who consists of consciousness, which is such that by it those two objects become related as the beneficiary and the benefactor; thus,
even though the two respective objects are sequential, they remain fixed within that very [will].

Because two things mounted upon a single cognition are grasped as one, their simultaneous manifestation in other forms is established by His will alone for the sake of worldly transaction; thus, there is no contradiction whatsoever.
Furthermore, that relationship exists only between two things, not among many; for regarding many things,
does it occur simultaneously with each individual one by means of multiple [relationships], or rather among the many as a whole?

In the middle, there is one for each one. In that regard, if each one is associated with multiple numbers, then are those multiple numbers themselves the objects of a single reflective awareness (*ekaparāmarśa*), or are they the objects of multiple reflective awarenesses? Or [is it that] the objects of multiple [awarenesses] are the objects of a single reflective awareness?
[This is an addition: "The king’s man," or "the king’s elephants, horses, chariots, and infantry.
Even in a *dvandva* compound, although there is multiplicity of elephants and so forth, because the referent (*parāmarśa*) is singular, the word itself is called a *dvandva*;
the words for elephants and so on are like [mere] phonemes (*varṇa*). For that which is situated in a single referent—

The word is one; because of the superimposition of that single word, the object is also one. For this very reason, these are the "entity-word-cognitions"—since the singular form of the compound's referent is feminine, its specific gender is not even mentioned. This word is exclusively feminine, and not [kha].

[The reading is *pu. nanviti*. This is a reference using a single-remainder compound (*ekaśeṣanirdeśa*), by which there would be a neuter single-remainder; and the plural number here is used with respect to the individual parts, as in the case of the word *dārāḥ* (wife/wives). Thus, in this [previous] case, the connection is indeed between two [things]. But here—
"The king's elephant, horse, chariot, and infantry"—

even though this constitutes the object of multiple distinct cognitions, there are as many [cognitions] of the king as there are cognitions of the elephant and so forth; thus, they serve solely to aggregate those [individuals].

The word "ca" [is used for this purpose]. Otherwise, in the absence of the word "ca," without the attraction (*anukarṣaṇa*) of the term "of the king" (*rājñaḥ*), the king—having become unified with the term "elephant" (*hastī*) through a single act of reference and being thus dependent upon it—would not undergo a renewed separation; and in that case, with what would the horses and so forth be connected?
Consequently, through metaphorical usage (*upacāra*), the grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) of the elephant and so forth is understood.
Alternatively,
since the conjunction is understood through the force of the context even in the absence of the word "and" (*ca*), that very same [entity] is each one individually.

The relationship between elephants and the other [animals] among themselves, as well as their being conjoined with respect to the action of existence (*sattā*), is illuminated by the word *ca* (and). Furthermore,
this manifestation of meaning is established in this way, and not otherwise.
It cannot be established as unapprehended, precisely because an appearance devoid of apprehension is impossible; for even in one who has set out upon the path...
The appearances of the touch, form, and so forth of objects such as grass situated at the side, which are devoid of reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*), cannot be admitted as existing,
because they lack the quality of being remembered; nor do they [exist] at that time.

The existence [of the self] established by inference is logical because of the presence of the causal complex consisting of the eye and other [senses], since there is no application of the mind [to those senses]. When that [application] exists, there is necessarily at that time the perception of grass and so forth, and now [at a later time] the recollection. And this [is explained] in the context of recognition (*pratyabhijñā*).
This has been established. And thus, it is logically consistent that the appearance of an object consists essentially of reflective awareness (*vimarśa*).

Just as there arises the reflective awareness, "Fire is in this smoke," so too for a refined cognizer (*pramātṛ*), there arises [the awareness] that "fire is the cause of this smoke" and "this smoke is the effect."

Thus, the function of manifestation regarding objects for cognitions culminates in their attaining a single nature; however, this does not conclude merely with their being manifest, but rather with their mutual cohesion.
The very reflection upon the mutual relationship of qualifier and qualified is itself the reflection upon the relationship consisting of the unity-in-multiplicity.
It is precisely this [reflection], permeated by the operation of the single reflective awareness, that constitutes the illusory [order] within the worldly transactions of transmigratory existence.

At that very moment, the cognizer cannot even admit the touch of another reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*), because for cognizers within the sphere of *māyā*, [all such awareness] consists of conceptual reflective awareness based on the differentiation of the non-recognition of the identity with Consciousness; this has also been elaborated upon in the *Īśvarapratyabhijñā*.

In legal procedure, since it is primarily the king or the individual who is sought to be known and intended to be informed, he alone is called the substantive (viśeṣya), while the other is the qualifier (viśeṣaṇa); thus, there is no inconsistency here either. And even though the two are identical, the qualifier—

In the expression "the king’s man" (*rājñaḥ puruṣaḥ*), the essential nature of the [king] shines forth as the qualified object (*viśeṣya*) while also appearing by way of its own nature. However, in the compound "king’s man" (*rājapuruṣaḥ*), the king, who has become the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*),
completely abandons his own nature and assumes exclusively the state of being the qualified object.
"It is manifested"—
thus, there is no linguistic expression of a relation in that case; this applies even to the phrase "a blue lotus."

In the expression "a blue lotus" (*nīlotpalam*), the lotus is primary, just like the quality "blue," which has entered into the interior of the lotus. In the case of "in a pot with wood-sticks" (*sthālyāṃ kāṣṭhaiḥ*), the pot and other factors appear as merged with the action that resides in the agent. Likewise, in the case of "the absence of a jar" (*ghaṭasyābhāvaḥ*), the absence [is primary].
In the conceptualizing cognition, the jar, being subsumed within [the cognition], appears as the primary object.

The meaning of "otherness" in the statement "this is other than that" is a qualified object (viśeṣya) which, without abandoning its own distinctness, has another, different object subsumed within itself.
In this way, it should be understood in all cases: in the relationship between action and its factors (kriyākāraka-sambandha)— [in the Kha manuscript,
the reading is "sambhinna"]—
there is an appearance of a relationship consisting of a temporary state of being the benefactor and the beneficiary.

But in the case of a remaining connection, it consists of the assistance being remembered; and even at the stage of remembrance, it is indeed the manifestation of an object previously perceived, because of the unity of the reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*), as has been stated. And not only this—
The activity of manifesting reality culminates in the limited subject, who is touched by the unity consisting of relations;
yet, at every moment, it rests solely in the manifestation of the infinite Śiva-nature composed of consciousness.

The activity of the cognition of an object does not involve a sequence; rather, in a single moment and in one and the same place, there is the manifestation of the object, and that very [manifestation] reveals its own nature as consisting of the state of Śiva, which is the essence of relationship—so it is said. And thus says the teacher Dharmakīrti:
And that cognition shines as being directed outward, appearing as the object;
whereas the cognition that grasps the intellect is always inwardly directed toward the Self.
Thus, by the words "introverted" and "in the Self," self-awareness is described as being devoid of the appearance of objects and as non-differentiated. Likewise,
it is stated in the *Pratyabhijñā*:
"And that very subject who is the nature of non-sequential, infinite consciousness—colored by the sequence of the objects of infinite intuition—is the Great Lord. (Īśvarapratyabhijñākārikā 1.7.1).
This has been demonstrated there at length. Furthermore, as for what was said regarding the time of cognition...
10) Thus, the admission of a relation is like the admission of a universal; for there is nothing whatsoever—whether this [relation] or anything else—that exists outside of cognition.

And the universal, though one, consists of many; even externally, it is distinct from the individual particulars (*svalakṣaṇa*) which constitute the collection of universals. And that [universal] is expressed by a single word as having as its basis various, unrestricted individual particulars.

That which is expressed is precisely that which is conveyed by a single word—such as "cow"—as being connected with an imagined specific characteristic (*kalpita-svalakṣaṇa*). For this very reason, the relation is called "inherence" (*samavāya*). This remains so even in the case of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*).

There is a single ultimate reality for both. In that case, one thing—the object—is what is expressed by the existential statement, such as "the blue lotus. Furthermore, the relation between the two is the identity of the qualified object (*viśeṣya*), and not the manifestation of some other distinct entity; this is the distinction. This remains true even in the case of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*).
Or, in the case of "a blue lotus," since the quality resides solely in the lotus as the qualified object, it is indeed a relation.
As for what was also said—that "the relation is the object of delusion because of its generality"—that too is stated far too little. For this entire universe...

This is precisely the state of delusion consisting of the non-apprehension of the non-difference from Consciousness. Furthermore, even within this delusion, there is no falsity—as in the case of a dream or a double moon—because it is consistent with reality;
all of this has been determined in the *Ṭīkā*. Thus it is.
Those who are incapable of reflecting upon the nature of the fullness of consciousness, yet— through attachment to that [limited] state alone—
reject the categories of relation and referent, are speakers of what is incoherent. (Thus it is said:)
Dependence and subordination do not constitute a relation between two insentient entities;
for even if their own existence were possible [as related], it would be a mere metaphorical usage and not a primary definition.
Because it is stated that non-existent things acquire their own nature, duality is thus abandoned;
in this way, the meaning of "relation" is established as nothing other than the conjunction of forms, and that [conjunction] exists. (2)
There is no immediate succession due to the lack of connection, as is the case with two iron rods;
therefore, the conjunction of multiple forms is indeed their identity as one.
"Just as others claim there is no sublation of the many even when there is unity in the one, so too entities are themselves unmixed; it is conceptual construction that joins them together. (4)
Since this is not merely a conceptual construction, it cannot be warded off;
its removal occurs through the cessation of the appearance, just as the delusion of a snake [is removed] by removing the [erroneous] perception.

For it is not because of being attached to an appearance, nor because of having an object similar to the appearance, but rather because of following after the appearance; that [object] is merely an erroneous appearance. (6)
In this very manifestation, where the manifold appears as one, the justification for the denotable object has also been clearly stated for the sake of recognition (pratyabhijñāna). || 7 ||
And this being so, it is not difficult to establish the unity of entities that, while existing as pure consciousness in essence, possess distinctions created by *māyā*. (8)
Even there, that which is the object of the worldly person's conceptualization belongs to the knower whose essence is difference in the form of the manifestation of non-difference from consciousness.
This activity, being obstructed by this [perception], cannot touch another conceptual construction;
for if it were to touch another conceptual construction, it would entail the consequence of a plurality of subjects (mātṛ). || 10 ||

Even though an object is manifold, it may proceed toward oneness by virtue of being superimposed with a single word through the operation of a single unifying cognition, just as in the case of "a pot and a cloth. (11)
Thus, there exists first of all another relation between the qualifier and the qualified;
it is for the purpose of mutual assistance, and that [relation] is useful to be known. (12)
Even when there is multiplicity, duality may exist between the qualifier and the qualified, just as a king’s horses, chariots, and infantry are the ground for the dual cognition [of "two"]. (13)
One [concept] is "the king's reflection," while another is directed toward its own universal;
this third is "the person" (puruṣa), which is capable of sustaining the relationship between the master and the universal. (14)
The expression "the king’s man" is an instance where the relation is grasped subsequently;
whether that relation is to be postulated by this [genitive] or both [the genitive and the noun] are to be postulated first, in every case these three [factors] are involved.
The relation denoted by the genitive case and so forth is situated within the qualifier.
Having attained oneness with the qualified object, it does not abandon its own form. || 16 ||
(14) Through the exclusion of one [of two possible relations], there occurs the connection of a subordinate element with another principal element when it is pure;
as for example, "the king's man" and "the Brahmin's [man]. (17)

Likewise, when a subordinate element attains oneness with another principal element, or with yet another, there occurs what is called a "connection" (saṃbandha) of the subordinate, as in the cases of "the king's horse" or "the king's man. (18)
Thus has been explained the process of connection; these cognitions, residing in the subject under the influence of māyā, perceive objects as distinct and set mundane activity in motion. (19)
Not only are all those [cognitions] deluded in that way, but they are also established at every moment in the infinite consciousness-reflection known as self-awareness (svasaṃvit). || 20 ||
Thus has been explained this uncontradicted and purposeful relationship established through self-awareness;
furthermore, the complete preparatory context for recognition is now presented.
Thus ends the *Saṃbandhasiddhi*, composed by the venerable teacher Utpaladeva, son of Udayākara.
By the command of the illustrious Lord of Kaśmīra, this [work] has been prepared and published by Madhusūdana Kaula for the delight of the virtuous.
